articles.title: Starnav takes delivery of Brazil-built hybrid offshore vessel
articles.summary: Starnav Serviços Marítimos has taken delivery of Starnav Elektra, the first hybrid platform supply vessel (PSV) designed and built in Brazil. The vessel was constructed by Detroit Brasil at its Itajaí shipyard and delivered to ABS class. The 92.1-metre vessel has a deadweight capacity of 5,500 tonnes and will operate...
articles.body: Starnav Serviços Marítimos has taken delivery of Starnav Elektra , the first hybrid platform supply vessel (PSV) designed and built in Brazil. The vessel was constructed by Detroit Brasil at its Itajaí shipyard and delivered to ABS class. The 92.1-metre vessel has a deadweight capacity of 5,500 tonnes and will operate under a long-term charter with Petrobras. It will support the company’s offshore logistics activities in Brazilian waters. The delivery is part of Starnav’s plans to expand its hybrid fleet. The company is planning a series of up to 10 vessels, including six PSVs and four oil spill response vessels. Battery system improves operational efficiency Starnav Elektra is equipped with a 1,322 kWh battery system that supports its dynamic positioning operations. If one engine fails, the batteries can keep the vessel in position for up to 20 minutes. This capability forms part of its DP2 requirements. The batteries are installed on the main deck, making them easier to access for maintenance. The system also allows the vessel to operate with fewer generators while maintaining the required safety margins. This can help reduce fuel consumption, emissions and engine maintenance. The vessel has received the ABS ESS-LiBATTERY, HYBRID and SUSTAIN-1 class notations. It is also designed to use renewable fuels such as hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO). With Starnav Elektra now delivered, Starnav has introduced battery-hybrid technology into its Brazilian offshore support operations. Further vessels are planned as part of the company’s fleet development programme.
takeaways: Starnav Serviços Marítimos has taken delivery of Starnav Elektra , the first hybrid platform supply vessel (PSV) designed and built in Brazil.

articles.body: Agility Global has agreed to sell its entire stake in energy logistics company Tristar to India’s Aegis Logistics in a transaction valued at US$1.5 billion. The deal values Tristar’s equity at US$882 million and is expected to close before the end of March 2027, subject to regulatory approvals. The enterprise valuation represents approximately six times Tristar’s 2025 EBITDA. The proposed acquisition would give Aegis Logistics control of an international energy logistics business with operations spanning maritime transport, road freight and fuel storage. Tristar operates across more than 30 countries Tristar has expanded from a regional road transport operator into a global energy logistics provider under Agility’s ownership. By 2025, the company operated in more than 30 countries, with a fleet of over 1,000 trucks and 26 ocean-going and coastal vessels. Its infrastructure also included 14 fuel storage facilities and more than 60 remote fuel sites. The company reported annual revenue of US$1.4 billion and EBITDA of US$257 million in 2025. Tristar’s expansion has included investments in maritime logistics and fuel storage. In 2022, it acquired a majority stake in Aquarius Energy, a joint venture with Glencore, adding exposure to a fuel storage platform with 3.5 million cubic metres of capacity. Agility prepares for another major divestment Agility acquired Tristar in 2003 for approximately US$7 million and invested a further US$123 million during the following seven years, including investments in fuel storage assets. According to Agility, its investment in the fuel logistics business is expected to generate a return exceeding US$1 billion over its 23-year holding period, representing an internal rate of return of approximately 16%. articles.title: LX Pantos opens logistics technology lab to advance robotics and AI
articles.summary: LX Pantos has opened a new technology laboratory at its MegaWise Cheongna Logistics Center in Incheon, South Korea, as the company expands its use of robotics and artificial intelligence in warehouse operations. The facility, known as the Technology-Driven Logistics (TDL) Lab, will test automation technologies and...
articles.body: LX Pantos has opened a new technology laboratory at its MegaWise Cheongna Logistics Center in Incheon, South Korea, as the company expands its use of robotics and artificial intelligence in warehouse operations. The facility, known as the Technology-Driven Logistics (TDL) Lab, will test automation technologies and assess how they can be integrated into daily logistics activities. The initiative focuses on improving warehouse processes, reducing manual work and developing more automated logistics centers. The project is part of LX Pantos’ wider strategy to strengthen its contract logistics business through robotics and AI. Seven technology partners support the initiative LX Pantos has established partnerships with seven technology companies to develop and test logistics automation solutions. The initiative began in April 2026, with the company signing memoranda of understanding with LG CNS, Hai Robotics, Libiao Robotics, XYZ Robotics, SUM, Twinny and Deepfine. The partnerships cover several areas of warehouse operations, including automated storage, order picking, parcel sorting and cargo handling. LG CNS will focus on integrated warehouse automation, while Hai Robotics and Libiao Robotics will contribute storage, picking and sorting technologies. XYZ Robotics will work on robotic solutions for container loading and unloading, alongside pallet handling. Other partners will support autonomous cargo transport, mobile robotics and vision-based inspection systems. The laboratory will allow LX Pantos to evaluate these technologies before introducing them into its wider logistics operations. articles.title: ENGIE and CMA CGM advance Le Havre biomethane project
articles.summary: ENGIE and CMA CGM have signed a framework agreement to develop a biomethane production facility in the industrial-port area of Le Havre, France. ENGIE will lead the project’s technical development and permitting process. Subject to a final investment decision, the energy group will also oversee the construction and...
articles.body: ENGIE and CMA CGM have signed a framework agreement to develop a biomethane production facility in the industrial-port area of Le Havre, France. ENGIE will lead the project’s technical development and permitting process. Subject to a final investment decision, the energy group will also oversee the construction and operation of the facility. From 2029, the plant is expected to supply CMA CGM’s fleet with 7,000 tonnes of biomethane annually, equivalent to approximately 100 GWh. The companies estimate that its use could avoid around 23,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions each year. The biomethane will be supplied through the European gas grid under a certified mass-balance system. It can be used by CMA CGM’s LNG-powered vessels without modifications to their engines or existing bunkering infrastructure. The facility will process livestock waste, household biowaste and agricultural residues. It is also expected to produce 100,000 tonnes of digestate for use as natural fertiliser and recover 13,000 tonnes of biogenic carbon dioxide for commercialisation. The development builds on the partnership established by ENGIE and CMA CGM in 2021 to support the production and distribution of renewable fuels for shipping. “With the construction of this new facility, we are pursuing our ambition to expand biomethane production capacity in support of the energy transition,” said Catherine MacGregor, Chief Executive Officer of ENGIE. “This partnership with CMA CGM demonstrates how industrial and energy players can work together to develop concrete solutions to decarbonise hard-to-electrify sectors, while strengthening energy sovereignty and the development of renewable gases,” she added. articles.title: China signs $336 million deal to build two container jetties at Bangladesh’s Mongla Port
articles.summary: After long delays, China has finally granted and signed a $336 million loan agreement with Bangladesh to build two container jetties at Mongla Port, the country’s second-largest seaport. The deal was signed in Dhaka on Monday, October 12, by Economic Relations Division (ERD) Joint Secretary Alia Meher on behalf of...
articles.body: After long delays, China has finally granted and signed a $336 million loan agreement with Bangladesh to build two container jetties at Mongla Port, the country’s second-largest seaport. The deal was signed in Dhaka on Monday, October 12, by Economic Relations Division (ERD) Joint Secretary Alia Meher on behalf of Bangladesh and EXIM Bank Assistant General Manager Fengjun Tian on behalf of China. A press statement issued by the ERD said China will charge 2% interest on the loan, as it is concessional credit. With the Chinese funding, Mongla Port will build two container jetties, each with a total length of 368 metres. A laden container yard spanning 87,600 square metres will also be built, along with a 34,170-square-metre empty container yard and a 4,260-square-metre hazardous cargo-handling yard. The funding will also be used to acquire modern equipment for the faster handling of containers and other cargo. Mongla Port officials said four gantry cranes, seven rubber-tyred gantry cranes and 33 other pieces of jetty-related equipment will be purchased under the project to modernise operations. The expansion of container and cargo-handling facilities with modern equipment will help increase Mongla Port’s annual handling capacity by 394,000 TEUs. The Chinese government nominated China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation (CCECC) as the project’s implementing agency. In June, Bangladesh and China signed a framework agreement to finance the construction of the Mongla Port project. Earlier, India had also pledged funding for the construction of jetties at Mongla Port. articles.body: Axpo has completed its first liquefied natural gas (LNG) bunkering operation at the Port of Valencia, Spain, supplying a container vessel with a fuel mix containing more than 50% bio-LNG. The ship-to-ship operation took place on 13 October 2026 using Axpo’s Alisios bunkering vessel, which has a capacity of 12,500 m³. The operation marks Axpo’s entry into LNG bunkering at Valencia, making it the fourth Spanish port where the company has provided the service. Previous operations took place in Málaga, Algeciras and Barcelona. The container vessel belongs to a major international transport and logistics company, although Axpo has not disclosed its name or the volume of fuel delivered. Expanding LNG bunkering services in Spain The latest operation forms part of Axpo’s expansion across major Mediterranean ports, where demand for alternative marine fuels is supporting the development of new bunkering services. The company launched Alisios in March 2026 at the Port of Huelva. The vessel operates along the southern Iberian coast, providing LNG and bio-LNG bunkering services to commercial ships. “As Spain’s largest port for container traffic and the fifth-busiest container port in Europe, Valencia is a strategically important location,” said Daniele Corti, Head of Small-Scale LNG at Axpo. Bio-LNG is produced from organic materials, including agricultural residues, biomass and waste. It can be used in LNG-powered vessels and offers potential lifecycle emissions benefits, depending on its production and supply chain. Growing presence across the Mediterranean Axpo began LNG bunkering operations in Málaga in April 2025 before expanding to Algeciras, Sines in Portugal and Barcelona. articles.title: Bluecore Energy secures nuclear fuel for maritime power development
articles.summary: Bluecore Energy has purchased low-enriched uranium for its first maritime nuclear energy system, marking progress in its plans to develop floating nuclear power technology. The US company acquired uranium hexafluoride (UF₆), enriched to 4.95% uranium-235, from WMC. The material is currently stored at a nuclear fuel...
articles.body: Bluecore Energy has purchased low-enriched uranium for its first maritime nuclear energy system, marking progress in its plans to develop floating nuclear power technology. The US company acquired uranium hexafluoride (UF₆), enriched to 4.95% uranium-235, from WMC. The material is currently stored at a nuclear fuel facility outside California. It will support future fuel production, testing and validation. The purchase follows Bluecore’s recent US$50 million seed financing. The company is also working with US regulators and the American Bureau of Shipping (ABS) as it develops its first system. Bluecore advances regulatory and certification work Bluecore began preliminary discussions with the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) in August 2026. The company presented its initial design and discussed the regulatory requirements for future deployment. The US Coast Guard also participated in the meeting. In June, Bluecore received Approval in Principle (AiP) from ABS for its floating nuclear power plant design. According to the company, this was the first such approval for a US-designed floating nuclear power plant. The approval provides a framework for further technical development. However, it does not represent final certification or permission to operate. Bluecore is now progressing with engineering, fuel qualification and safety assessments. These activities will support the next stages of testing and regulatory review. Floating nuclear power for ports and coastal facilities Bluecore is developing its technology at its headquarters within the Port of Long Beach. The company is currently working on a reactor module prototype that does not contain nuclear fuel. Its compact, water-cooled systems are being designed for installation on floating platforms.
